titulo: The order of operations at the counter
subtitulo: Where to stand, how loud to be, and the permission to stop being so polite that nobody serves you
cena: Three people who arrived after you have already been served, and you are still standing back waiting to be noticed.
frasePiso: Get to the counter, catch the eye, say the thing. Politeness that keeps you invisible is not politeness here.
decisao: chegar ao balcão e falar em volume normal em vez de esperar ser notado, porque no bar italiano esperar educadamente é ficar sem café

steps.pt: An Italian bar has no queue and no system, and that is not chaos. It is a different system, and you can learn it in one part.
Step one: go to the counter. Not near it. People are served in the order they make eye contact, not in the order they arrived.

steps.acao: That was directed at you. Answer immediately — hesitating passes your turn to someone else.

steps.promptPt: Claim the turn and order in one breath. Speak now.
steps.es: A me, grazie. Un caffè e un cornetto.
steps.pinyin: a meh, GRA-tsee-eh. oon kaf-FEH eh oon kor-NET-to
steps.pt: Me, thanks. A coffee and a croissant.
steps.tts: A me, grazie. Un caffè e un cornetto.

steps.pt: A chi tocca means whose turn. Answering a me is not pushy — it is the expected reply, and silence hands your place away.

steps.promptPt: Someone jumped ahead of you. Say it was your turn, calmly. Speak now.
steps.es: Scusi, credo che toccasse a me.
steps.pinyin: SKOO-zee, KRE-do keh tok-KAS-se a meh
steps.pt: Sorry, I think it was my turn.
steps.tts: Scusi, credo che toccasse a me.

steps.pt: Step two is the till. Many bars want payment first, and the receipt is what buys you the drink at the counter.

steps.promptPt: Ask whether you pay first, before joining the wrong side. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do you pay at the till first?

steps.acao: Pay, take the receipt, and put it on the counter where the barista can see it.
steps.es: Sì, poi porta lo scontrino qui al banco.
steps.pt: Yes, then bring the receipt here to the counter.
steps.tts: Sì, poi porta lo scontrino qui al banco.

steps.promptPt: Ask for water with the coffee, using the frame from B14. Speak now.
steps.pt: Could you bring me a glass of water?
About cappuccino after eleven: order it whenever you like. Nobody will stop you, and some of them will notice. Both are true.

steps.promptPt: It is four in the afternoon and you want one anyway. Order it. Speak now.
Order the one Italians actually drink after a meal — an espresso with a drop of milk. Speak now.
steps.pt: An espresso with a drop of milk, please.

steps.promptPt: You are ordering for two people. Say it in one go. Speak now.
steps.pt: Two coffees, one with a drop of milk.

steps.promptPt: Two minutes and you are done. Close it on the way out. Speak now.

steps.es: A me, grazie. Un caffè e un cornetto. Si paga prima alla cassa? Grazie, buona giornata!
steps.pinyin: a meh GRA-tsee-eh. oon kaf-FEH eh oon kor-NET-to. see PA-ga PREE-ma AL-la KAS-sa. GRA-tsee-eh BWO-na jor-NA-ta
steps.pt: Shadow the whole counter transaction, start to finish.
steps.tts: A me, grazie. Un caffè e un cornetto. Si paga prima alla cassa? Grazie, buona giornata!

steps.pt: I02 done. Go to the counter, answer a chi tocca with a me, check the till, and be out in two minutes.

secoes.titulo: A chi tocca is the whole system
secoes.corpo: The bar staff track arrival order loosely and ask when they lose it. Answering a me is participating correctly; waiting to be picked out is what puts you fourth in a queue that does not exist.

exemplos.es: Scusi, credo che toccasse a me.
exemplos.pt: Sorry, I think it was my turn.

secoes.corpo: Charging before serving is entirely lawful, and both systems are in use: pay-first is common in busy urban bars, order-first and settle on the way out is common in smaller towns. The printed sign asking you to make the scontrino at the till is the tell, and watching the person ahead of you is free.

There is a genuine convention that milky coffee belongs to the morning, and there is no rule, no hour and no refusal. Italian trade writing calls the story of the barista who says no «a travellers' legend», and the digestive reasoning behind the habit is belief rather than physiology. What Italians do is simply not order one. Order what you want, and know the convention exists — that is a different thing from obeying it.

The counter coffee is designed to take two minutes: order, drink, pay, leave. That speed is why it costs what it costs, and it is also why hovering back from the counter reads as not being in the transaction yet.

permissao: You are allowed to speak up at a counter. Stepping forward and saying a me at normal volume is not rudeness in an Italian bar — it is how the room works, and the version where you wait politely to be noticed ends with you leaving without coffee.
espelho: Anyone who has stood at a busy bar at home and watched two later arrivals get served first knows this feeling exactly. The instinct to wait your turn is right in most places and wrong in this one, which is the only thing that makes it hard.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You are standing a polite step back from the counter and people who came in after you keep getting served.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They are being rude, or the staff are ignoring foreigners.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Service at an Italian bar runs on proximity and eye contact rather than on an ordered queue. Standing back is read as not being ready yet, so the staff move to whoever is signalling that they are.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Move to the counter, look at the barista, and answer a chi tocca with a me, grazie followed immediately by your order.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You are served in about the order you arrived, and the two-minute transaction the format is built around actually takes two minutes.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not where there is a visible ticket machine or a marked queue — pharmacies, delicatessen counters, post offices and some bakeries run on numbers, and ignoring those is genuinely rude.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: The rule that cappuccino cannot be ordered after 11 is a habit, not a prohibition. The digestive reasoning behind it is a cultural belief rather than a physiological finding, there is no precise hour — the real line is «after breakfast» — and Italian trade sources describe the flat refusal by a barista as «una leggenda da viaggiatori», a travellers' legend. What Italians actually do is not order one.
fatosDatados.fonte: Pasqualini il Caffè — «Il cappuccino dopo le 11: regola, mito o snobismo tutto italiano»

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Requiring payment before consumption at a bar is lawful: bars, pastry shops and gelaterie may demand payment at the cassa first, and the receipt records the payment rather than the delivery of the service. Both systems coexist — pay-first is common in busy urban bars, especially in the north, while smaller towns tend to order first and pay on leaving. The tell is a printed sign asking for the scontrino to be made at the till before consuming.
fatosDatados.fonte: Cookist — «Ricevuta prima di andare al banco: i bar possono chiedere il pagamento anticipato?»
